utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the accused resumes his cross-examination, you can see I'm assisted this morning by Mr. Theunens. I draw this to your attention. He's one of the members of the OTP who has assisted in the preparation of this witness, but he is, in due course, going to be, or expected to be an expert witness is coming from the military analysis department of the Tribunal and for those reasons I thought I'd better put it on the record that he's actually in court today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, General, let's round off what we were discussing about the competence of the -- of Yugoslavia towards the armies of Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina. Is it true and correct that Yugoslavia did not have any competencies with respect to command of those armies -- over those armies?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In which period?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout the whole period. The material time. The period you're testifying about. If somebody else has something else to add I'll ask them.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I explained that the Territorial Defence in the territory of Kninska Krajina was subordinated and under the command of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until the JNA withdrew pursuant to the Vance Plan; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, once the JNA withdrew from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the territory of the Republika Srpska Krajina according to the Vance Plan, and once the armies of Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina had been formed, or the Serbian army of Krajina, did the JNA have any power and authority over the commands over those armies?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the JNA didn't exist then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the army of Yugoslavia then have any authority over those armies?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I wasn't an active-duty officer to be able to answer that question directly, but I can give you some information which I knew about and some data that I learnt about from the officers and superior officers who, from the army of Yugoslavia, went to join up with the army of Republika Srpska or Republika Srpska Krajina then once again returned to the army -- to the JNA. And I know about the presence of top figures from what we call the Vojna Linija, or military line, which during the Pauk operation, Operation Pauk, were at the command post from which they were able to command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him finish. Do not interrupt him. Yes, General. Continue his answer. He is answering your question about the information we had. Now, is there anything you want to add, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, just to finish the sentence I had started. So some of these top people were in the most forward command post for the Operation Pauk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I was asking you something quite directly, and that was did the army of Yugoslavia have any command responsibility over the army of Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina? I didn't ask you whether it was a good year for plums or whether anybody had come visiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Mr. Milosevic, that's a totally unfair comment. Now, he's answered the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Had you asked me about plums, I would have told you about the plum situation. But you asked me whether Yugoslavia participated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: General, don't. You'll only keep things going. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Ask some further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I asked was did the army of Yugoslavia have any competencies and command authority over the army of Republika Srpska, army of Republika Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And my answer was that I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not know. I know about the details that I told you of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you don't know that they had their headquarters and staff and supreme commands? You know nothing about that? You know nothing about who appointed the various commanders in the army of Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina? You know nothing of any of that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do know about that, but I don't know or, rather, I do know that the ranks that were given had to be verified later on in Yugoslavia. And I also know, and let me repeat once again, and this is not linked to the army of Yugoslavia, that some of the top people from MUP assumed command positions in Operation Pauk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, well, you seem to have focused your attention on that MUP. Whatever the subject, your answer is MUP.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what the situation was like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. We'll come to that. We'll get to that, and we'll have other questions too linked to that particular issue. But you said here, and I made a note of it, I wrote down your words, you said that a parallel army had been established from the MUP and that MUP, you used the word, became an armada. That's the word you used. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't emphasise it the way you're doing now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But you did use the word "armada," didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not use the word "armada." That is not a term that I use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, look at the LiveNote and you'll be able to see for yourself, and people in Yugoslavia watched all this. But tell us, how big did the MUP get? How massive did it become, and how was this parallel army in fact formed, and how far was MUP at all, because you say -- you claim that -- how many members did MUP have at all?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm keeping that piece of information as confidential, as secret, an official secret, and I assume that you can give us a better answer to that. But from the information and data and indices presented here during the presentation of evidence, we saw that intervention brigades did exist, that detachments did exist, that they had helicopters, that they had APCs, armoured vehicles, and that is something that they did not previously have. And you saw on the basis of the request that was made, and you and I observed that it was a megalomaniac request, asking for the Banja Luka SUP to provide technical resources and materiel which was the materiel of a military brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the MUP of Serbia ask for that, request that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the MUP of Serbia, but you know full well that the MUP of Serbia received from the army --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, General. Just a moment. Let's make things clear. Would you please answer my questions.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you keep interrupting me and I'm not able to provide an answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I can't ask you one thing and have you answer something quite different. What I'm asking you is how big this MUP was, because you keep focusing on MUP and calling it an armada and things of that kind. So how big was it in fact?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't have any official data of information, but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, give us an example.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was publicised that there were about 90.000 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all right. That's what I'm telling you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it unfortunate that a general, head of the intelligence service, has to use data and information that he has heard bandied about and rumoured in the streets, round the back corners of the streets and in cafes? Is this serious testimony for you to quote a figure of 90.000 men?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, don't hold me to my word. I'm sure you will have facts and figures which will show you what the state of affairs was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I do have them.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then provide them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's why I say it's shameful for you to claim something like that.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not working in the MUP intelligence for me to be able to have the kind of data that you have as president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I see that you had -- did your intelligence work vis-a-vis along the lines of just one member of MUP, and then you say you didn't deal with intelligence work for the whole of MUP.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't. These are facts and figures and information that would come to us periodically from people who were sent away by people like that, and I assume you knew that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say harassed. Who harassed these people and sent them away?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, are we in open session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know about the officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you want to go into closed session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That would be a good idea. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am opposed. I object.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, General. I have some data for 1991, also for 1995, and this terrible police, this armada, et cetera, the maximum strength it had in 1995 numbered 32.000. That is not counting the state security, and the entire state security department had a total of 3.500 employees. And these 32.000, out of this figure, 3.000 were firemen who are also employees of the Ministry of the Interior. Six thousand are administrative personnel. As you know, they issue passports, driving licenses, and many other administrative tasks; typists, secretaries, technicians, et cetera. The police with general competencies, the people in the street to maintain the law and order, patrolmen, numbered 14.000. I'm talking about 1995. In 1991, there were only 10.000. The traffic police, 3.000. The frontier police, 3.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness must have a chance to answer all these figures. General, is there anything you want to say on what's been put to you so far?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This probably -- these figures apply to the permanent police force and not including the reserve force. That is the first point. The second is perhaps it would be interesting to give the figures for 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I do have the figures for 1999. They are spectacularly different. They really are. A total of 36.000; 6.000 in administration, 3.500 firemen - so they went up by 500 - 3.000 crime police members, 3.500 frontier policemen - they were increased by 500 too - 4.000 traffic policemen, and 16.000 policemen of general competence, including special police units that you are referring to. And do you know that, General, that they consisted of policemen working at their work posts, and then when a special unit is formed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... you're now going on to a separate point. General, you should be able to deal with the figures which have been put. Is there anything you want to say about them before we come to the special units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not have occasion to have such data or to have access to them to be able to enumerate the numbers regarding policemen and firefighters and all the rest. But I don't know the unit that I mentioned, to whom it belonged, the Skorpions. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They reported to you on the 17th of May. What did you -- I report about?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I referred to at the private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. You were reporting that there was a volunteer unit somewhere.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not volunteer. Members of SAJ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was called a special anti-terrorist unit and not Scorpios. So I'm asking you about the Scorpios in that unit.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. Someone may call himself what they will, but a special anti-terrorist unit has its own formation and it is well known what its name is, just like Arkan's unit which had its own name too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Arkan was never in Kosovo during the war of 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where Arkan was, but I was speaking about men from his unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as far as I understand it, the men who were with him as members of volunteer units applied as volunteers, and according to information I received then that you are now testifying about - I don't remember it but you have said it and let's accept it - that only 30 of them were admitted as volunteers and the rest were turned back precisely because of certain problems that the competent organs thought there might be with them. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what I said. Not quite the way you put it. Among other things, it was said that the previous day they had killed people. That is the first point. Secondly, Mr. Sainovic did not know that Arkan's units were in Kosovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please answer my question. You keep mentioning Sainovic. As you know, Sainovic was the vice-premier, the vice-president of the federal government. And by the federal government, being the vice-president of that government, he was assigned responsibility for Kosovo and Metohija. During the OSCE presence, he was president of the Yugoslav Commission for Cooperation with them. He negotiated with Rugova and other politicians over there. He held a series of political meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What you must do is ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking a question. If he said he was not aware of that unit, why wouldn't you believe him? Do you believe that he was not telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm just saying that it was strange that he didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if he didn't know, how could I know?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should have known from Rade Markovic, who told you about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to what you say, he passed on this information at a meeting that Sainovic was present at, and Sainovic said that he didn't know about it. Did that happen then?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described a meeting, but we'll come back to that meeting. That was in public session, and you'll be able to answer questions about it. You described the meeting, and you said Rade Markovic said that there were 30 men, volunteers, which they had accepted, and that the others had been turned back, and that Sainovic said - when I asked what about this - that Sainovic said that he was not aware of it, so how could I have known if he didn't know about it? And he learnt about it, if what you're saying is correct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not for the witness to answer what you knew or didn't know, what you could have known and what you couldn't have known. He's described what happened. Now, you were asking questions earlier. I think we had got onto Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll come to that meeting, as the witness diluted it rather, so we'll review it in its integrity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But let us focus for a moment on the police. As you see, quite incorrect figures have been given by you regarding the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given his answer to that. He's given his answer. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the relative ratio of policemen in Serbia in 1995, for instance, not in 1991, the ratio of policemen to the population was 1 to 434 citizens? This is counting all those employed in the police. I don't know whether in other countries they count the firefighters and the administrative officers and everything. In France, it is 1 to 266. In Italy, 1 to 338. In Holland, in Britain. Only Japan has a lower ratio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the point? What is the point?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The point is that there is a rumour being spread here of a very strong police force in Serbia, whereas in fact the police force in Serbia was smaller than in virtually all other European countries in relation to the population. And Serbia was in a wartime environment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not -- we're not in fact using the time very usefully. You can call your evidence about that, but you know what the witness says. He says that that doesn't include the reservists, the reserve forces who, the evidence is, were in action. Now, whether they were or not is something which we may have to decide, but there's no good arguing with the witness whether there were a lot or not a lot of policemen. We've gone as far as we can on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The reserve force could only exist in wartime, and the witness is talking about 1991 and 1992, and you too are referring to that period. Therefore, gentlemen, these are things that cannot be compared.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I comment briefly? From the figures that you have given, in 1991 there were about 10.000 people employed in the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said in 1991, there were 22.000 total, not counting the state security which was always constant at the level of 3.500, whereas the general competence police numbered 10.000, traffic 2.000, frontier 2, crime 3, firefighters 2.000 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness -- we've heard these figures. Let the witness finish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's say 20.000. Again, it was doubled. But that is not the point I'm making in this discussion. In 1992, that is in the month of March, the standing force of the JNA in those days had a total of 36.000. So compare the number of employed in MUP to those in the army, and I'm saying that they were more or less equal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How can you say such things as a general? A policeman is employed, and a soldier is not an employee. The police doesn't have soldiers who are unemployed and serving as part of their national service. You're talking about the employees in the army who are officers and non-commissioned officers, professional soldiers who receive a salary. In the police -- in the police, all policemen are professionals. There are no conscripts in the police, doing their military service. Therefore, the army mostly consists of conscripts doing their national service, and the minority are officers. Unless you're saying that there are more officers than soldiers. I'm giving you the total number of the employed in the Ministry of the Interior, including the administration, including the technicians, the firefighters, and everyone else. You said 90.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us deal with it in this way: Mr. Milosevic, as usual, you argue with the witness. That's not what you're here to do. Now, General, is there anything you want to add to what you've said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the number of permanently employed in the MUP and the number of permanently employed in the whole of the Yugoslav People's Army was such that there were more in the MUP than in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, give us the figures, please. What was the total number of staff in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thirty-six thousand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see, 36.000. What year?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 27th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The whole of the JNA. Fine. I'll take that figure as your claim, as I have to save time. I just wish, before passing on to some concrete questions which you should be well-informed about, to ask you the following: Was it the top military leadership in 1991, Veljko Kadijevic -- I'm now talking about the ethnic composition. He was a Yugoslav. Blagoje Adzic, chief of the Main Staff, a Serb from Bosnia-Herzegovina. So cadres from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Josip Gregoric, deputy and under-secretary from Croatia, a Croat. Stane Brovet, a deputy federal secretary, a Slovene. Mile Ruzinovski, Chief of Staff of the first administration - this is the operations administration and the most one - a Macedonian. The commander of the north-western theatre of operations, Konrad Kolsek, a command post in Zagreb, a Slovene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you reading this. You're supposed to be asking questions. General, if at any stage you disagree with anything that's being said, just interrupt, because it's the only way we can deal with it. Do you agree so far with what the accused has read out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The -- what he has read out is correct, and it applies to the first half of 1992 and not to the subsequent period. In more concrete terms, General Gregoric was pensioned off, and he was replaced by General Sljivic. General Kolsek was also replaced as commander of the 5th Military District, and General Avramovic came to take his place, Zivota Avramovic. Then General Ruzinovski was replaced when he was sent as commander of the 2nd Operative Group to Eastern Herzegovina, and only a few days after that, because of his alleged reaction to the fact that Montenegrins over there and other people who were there would not allow a Macedonian to be their commander. And let me not go on enumerating, but these are the facts. On the 4th of December in 1991, 41 per cent of the total staff in the air force, and I'm only talking about the air force, were not Serbs and Montenegrins; they were people of all ethnicities. There were 2 per cent Hungarians, 1 per cent Albanian. And regarding the actual flyers, the pilots, 52 per cent were Serbs and Montenegrins, and 48 per cent were people of other ethnicities. However, that picture in the subsequent period, that is during the second half of 1992 and 1993, changed significantly so that, on various grounds, people were replaced because they didn't have citizenship and they now belong to other states. Some stayed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But let me -- please answer my question first and then we'll move on and you can make any additional remarks if you have any. This list that I've read out to you so far, is it correct? I'm asking you, is it correct for 1991? Is it correct or not? Don't explain what happened later. We'll come to the reasons for the changes.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I'm giving you a different picture for the end of 1991. That is also 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you care about the picture? I'm asking you whether this is correct.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not correct in the way you're interpreting it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Aleksandar Spirkovski, a Macedonian, was not the commander of the central theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When, when, when?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not until the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop this. I'm going to stop this for a moment. Read out what you say the position was for 1991 and we'll hear that and then we'll go on to deal with later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let him challenge any name. I'm going to read this out to you. I'm going to read out 16 names. 1, Veljko Kadijevic, Federal Secretary. 2, Blagoje Adzic, Chief of General Staff. Josip Gregoric, deputy federal secretary and under-secretary. Stane Brovet, deputy, federal secretary, under-secretary. Mile Ruzinovski, head of the first administration of the General Staff. That is the cooperative -- that is the operative administration. Konrad Kolsek -- I'll slow down. Konrad Kolsek, commander of the north-west battlefield. The commanders in Zagreb: Spirkovski, commander of the central theatre, headquarters in Belgrade. Andrija Silic, also a Croat, Chief of Staff of the central theatre. Zivota Avramovic, head of the south-east theatre, headquarters in Skopje. Bozidar Grubisic, head of the navy. Anton Tus, head of the air force. Zvonko Jurjevic, deputy chief of the air force. So when Tus was pensioned off, as you said, again, he was replaced by a Croat, Jurjevic. Ivan Radanovic, head of the centre for higher military schools in Belgrade. Ibrahim Alibegovic, head of the war college. Tomislav Bjondic, commander of the Command Staff Academy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What nationality or ethnicity are you saying they had?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the way it was: Kadijevic, Yugoslav; Adzic, Serb from Bosnia; Josip Gregoric, Croat; Stane Brovet, Slovenian; Mile Ruzinovski, Macedonian; Konrad Kolsek, Slovenian; Aleksandar Spirkovski, Macedonian; Andrija Silic, Croat; Zivota Avramovic, Serb; Bozidar Grubisic, Croat; Anton Tus, Croat; Zvonko Jurjevic, Croat; Ivan Radanovic, Croat; Ibrahim Alibegovic, Muslim; Tomislav Bjondic, Croat; Mate Petar, a Croat. The ethnic pattern as regards these 16 top generals in the top military echelon of the JNA: One Yugoslav, two Serbs -- that is to say from Bosnia and Serbia proper, a total of two Croats, eight Slovenians, two Macedonians too, and Muslims one. Did I have any influence over this top military echelon? You tell me that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're going on to a totally different point. First of all, let's deal with the list as it's been read out, since the general is giving evidence and not you. Is the list which the accused has read out correct for 1991 or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for one period in 1991, the first half of 1991, as regards some persons. As regards some other persons, it is relevant to the period up to September 1991. Bozidar Grubisic was not, in 1991, commander of the navy. He was Assistant Federal Secretary for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For what?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For personnel. Political affairs, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, it's not correct that Grubisic was commander of the navy in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Another admiral who was a Serb. I can't remember his last name right now, but it's not that it really matters. And his Chief of Staff was a Croat. Bozo Erceg. Out of those who have been mentioned, the following have been replaced: As I said, General Ruzinovski, immediately a few days after being appointed commander of the 2nd Operative Group, at the request of Montenegro, as far as I know, that he is not accepted as this kind of an appointment because he's Macedonian. Then General Spirkovski was replaced by Zivota Panic who was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. appointed. Andrija Silic was replaced and later on, he was detained and investigations were carried out against him in 1993. Then General Kolsek was replaced and Zivota Avramovic took his place. And I could go on referring to these replacements and other appointments, however, I cannot give a clear-cut answer. If one says 1991, this situation was partially true. But as I said, either up to June 1991 or by September, at the latest, when all these changes were made and when retirements took place. But General Zvonko Jurjevic did not come to become Deputy Chief of Staff for the air force. He was commander of the air force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not saying that. He was deputy head of the air force. He was Tus's deputy. And then when Tus left, he came to his position. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. In the army this is called the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, all right. He was the number 2 person in the air force; is that right? Tus was commander, Jurjevic was Chief of Staff. Both of them Croats. When Tus retired, the then Chief of Staff Jurjevic became commander. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So a Croat was there before him, he retired, and then again a Croat came to the position of commander of the air force.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And on the 25th of September, 1991, an effort was made to carry out a coup in the air force. Bozidar Stefanovic was behind it, and they tried to get rid of Zvonko Jurjevic in this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, please. What did you challenge out of this entire list that I read out to you? Only that Grubisic was not commander of the navy but, rather, Assistant Federal Secretary for National Defence. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I gave my answer. If you didn't understand it, I'm not going to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there something else that is incorrect in this list? You claim that Grubisic was not at this position?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What period are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1991, General.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which month? The year has 12 months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about 1991.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is an imprecise question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what hour, minute, and day people -- until what minute, hour, and day people held their appointments. I have this list and I'm asking you whether it's correct.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said for which period this list was correct and in what respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, so towards the end of 1991 Kadijevic was no longer Federal Secretary for National Defence, Blagoje Adzic was no longer Chief of Staff, and let's go on.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they or were they not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 8th of January, Kadijevic was Secretary for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Adzic throughout 1991?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't challenge any of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what are you challenging?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, go on. Go on. Move on to Spirkovski.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I read you this list for 1991.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's fine. But you're asking me about Blagoje Adzic. Why don't you ask me about Spirkovski?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't have time to. I read out all the names to you and I don't have time to go from one name to another, I'm not going to go into all of that, I'm just asking you about 1991 when these conflicts started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has answered. Now what he should have, in fairness to him, is the list in front of him so that he could begin to answer it. If you want to ask any more questions about it, then you'll have to put a copy of it in front of him, or the original.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will deal with that. That's not a problem for the witness either. He's just trying to be of such great assistance to this Prosecution that even what is undeniable he is trying to challenge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic. Comments do not assist. Just get on with the questions. If you want him to have a copy of the list, he can have it. Otherwise, we'll move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we go back to that, I'll give him the copy. Actually, somebody can take this and this copy -- this can be copied.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, I don't really need a copy of this. I know all of this by heart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it's probably just as well the Court has a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, if possible, can you just give me brief answers to my questions, because my time will be limited. I'm going to put an entire series of questions to you that have to do with the period that you're testifying about and concerning events that you should know something about. Is it correct that after the victory of the HDZ in the elections in 1990 that over there various expert teams were immediately established for military matters?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that a project of the Croat armed forces was carried out then, counting on 44.000 people for all the arms and services, that is to say the army, navy, and ground forces?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that on the basis of that project a plan of special activity vis-a-vis JNA officers was worked out, especially those who were ethnic Croats, with a view to breaking up the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that Boljkovac then stated that Croatia is prepared to sacrifice 25.000 people in order to attain these objectives?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that in mid-1990 a meeting was held between the delegation of the HDZ and the Slovenian Demos precisely in order to agree on what their tactics vis-a-vis the JNA would be in order to have broken up?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a meeting then, and there was another meeting in January 1991 in Otocac Krka. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that on the basis of the agreement reached then, that you have confirmed, the leaderships of the HDZ and Demos, on the 9th of July, 1990, Slovenia started preparations for establishing its own army? And Jelko Kacin, the Deputy Minister of Defence of Slovenia, in the centre for training the TO near Ljubljana, said that Slovenia already in September would sent to the federal authorities an ultimatum that 60 per cent of conscripts should serve their military service in Slovenia, 35 per cent in Croatia, and only 5 per cent in the rest of the SFRY, and that already in December of that year 90 per cent of the conscripts would remain in Slovenia and 10 per cent would be in Croatia. Do you remember these figures?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is 1990?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also correct that Kacin said at that meeting that if the federal authorities do not meet this request, Slovenia would stop paying into the federal budget and it will also tell all Slovenian officers to leave the JNA in order for the Slovenian army to be established?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that this was coordinated with the leadership of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that at that time what was agreed upon was that all powers of the federal states should be taken over in the domain of defence and that all of this should be put under their own authority, that a detailed cleansing of personnel and secretariats should be carried out, Secretariats of National Defence, also in the Territorial Defence, in the Ministry of Interior, and that at all offices in these ministries tested personnel who are ethnic Croats and Slovenians respectively should be appointed?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that in the -- in mid-1990 in Croatia, that is to say in 1990, mid-1990, that what started was the massive establishment of volunteer units in order to replace the Territorial Defence which was multi-ethnic and that this, in mid 1990, preceded the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about information from mid -- mid-July 1990 when volunteer units were established that were then called the Croatian National Guard Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we are talking about mid-1990. Let's not split any hairs now, 15 days here or there. Is it correct that in mid-June 1990, mid-June 1990 in Croatia, a campaign was launched to replace the top personnel of the TO? About 60 per cent of all personnel were replaced. And within that campaign of replacing the top personnel of the TO, on the 25th of June, 1990, Spegelj sent a telegram to all in the TO related to the change of personnel because there was resistance to such policy, and then he informs them in this telegram and he makes it compulsory upon them to cleanse the personnel of the TO, and in this sense they should closely coordinate with the leaders of the municipalities. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that telegram. I'm not sure about the actual date and the month that you are referring to, but I do know about the personnel purges in the Ministry of Defence of Croatia. When General Spegelj became minister, he immediately dismissed 20 employees who were primarily ethnic Serbs, and this fits into the context that you are referring to now, but I don't know exactly which month this was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that through HDZ committees and the Catholic church, these volunteer units were enlisting their personnel?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Checks were made for the personnel for these volunteer units. It is either the Catholic church or the local committees of the HDZ that were checking them out and giving recommendations for them. I don't know whether they were actually carrying out the recruitment, but the Catholic church, inter alia, said who was eligible to enlist in these units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that at that time, from Western Herzegovina, 220 members were received from there because Croatia already considered Western Herzegovina to be their territory at that time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we -- we had that kind of information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that among the persons who were engaged were many persons who were sentenced to many years in prison for having committed grave crimes, as well as those who had not done their military service? So in order to -- in Valdanos, Lucka, Zagreb, Rakic, all prisoners were released, all of those who were serving prison sentences for grave crimes like looting, murder, et cetera? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, say what it was.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not in Valdanos but in Valbadon, near Pula. And also the other places that you mentioned, these were not prisons, these were camps for training and for having these units that were established stationed. So in Lucka, there was not a prison, this was a MUP base. So these were not prisons. What is true is that there was one prison, Valbadon, near Pula. Valdanos is on the southern coast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. There may be a mistake as far as the name is concerned, but is it correct that it is precisely these persons who were serving prison sentences were engaged there? Is it true that criminals were recruited? I'm talking about the actual phenomenon.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Just like in some military units in Serbia there were also criminals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I understand your need to explain straight away that there was something of that kind in Serbia. I'm sure there is in France and England, but I'm asking about Croatia specifically now. Is it true that at that time or, rather, on the 27th of July, 1990 we're talking about, a competition was published to take in MUP personnel on condition that the candidates were morally and politically reliable, could be trusted, and so on and so forth? So that all those who were recruited secretly were later on turned in to these orderlies of the ZNG, Croatian National Guard Corps, and stationed in the training centre in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the situation was a little different. First of all, data was published in the Belgrade press as to the formation of the Croatian guards. And I think that this was on the 25th of July, 1990. And then two reactions that came with the establishment of this organisation: The MUP who had taken in these people earlier on, previously, into these illegal volunteer units covered them by publishing a subsequent competition on the 27th of July, whereas the competition was published as it was in the Socialist Republic of Croatia, which implied moral and political reliability, trustworthiness, and so on. So there was this job vacancy that was publicised and that was the competition. And the condition was that they had done their military service. So until this job announcement came up, they tried to legalise -- with this competition and job announcement, they tried to legalise the people who they had taken in earlier. So this centre, this educational training centre, was not the only thing and existed in these facilities in Zagreb but in the other places that you said were prisons and were not prisons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you mean the institutions of higher learning.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's make one thing clear: The fact that was publicised about these illegal formations was correct, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when they saw that everything had been made public and come out into the open because the press had been writing about it, they hurried up to legalise the illegal situation that had been created previously; is that what you're saying? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that, in that period of time, those units had already been armed with automatic weapons?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which period are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the period of time that we're talking about, that is to say mid-1990 or, rather, July to be more exact. Let me put myself right and say July 1990.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about the period from the end of September or the beginning of October, I know that for certain, that they did have automatic weapons. What weapons they had before that, I can't say. But as of the end of September and beginning of October, from the contingent of weapons that had been imported and brought in from Hungary, these formations were armed, yes. What they had been using for weapons before that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that at that time the Territorial Defence in Croatia was selected on an ethnic basis, already at that time, that its members were selected on an ethnic basis in the middle of the year?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- no. The Territorial Defence was not, especially the republican staff and headquarters. Again General Ostovic was still there, he was a Croat. However, the Secretariats for National Defence, which were under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Defence, something was done there and the cadres were sifted through and vetted. Now, whether in some Municipal Staff of the Territorial Defence some of this vetting took place, I really can't say, but in the Secretariat for National Defence, that was true; it did happen there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And is it true that from June 1990, Croatia, to all intents and purposes, intensively worked to establish its own army, to form its own army, and that there was intensive training of these formations and the aim was on marksmanship?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They started their training with marksmanship, as far as I know, and they represented this as being as the members were the police. But as I know, the police -- and guardsmen. But the police, first of all, learns about rules and regulations and then how -- and then learns how to use weapons. With them, it was the reverse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true, General, that in August 1990, Vladimir Seks, Ivan Vekic, Branimir Glavas -- do you know those names? I assume you do.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they all top functionaries of the HDZ? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The new authorities in Croatia. That was what they were. And in August 1990, they agreed to form the armed section or armed detachments, in fact, armed detachments on the territory of the Sremska Baranja region, and the formation of groups for silent liquidation.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know for certain is this: I know about Glavas. He was the Secretary for National Defence in Osijek. And I know that Mercep, Mercep's group, in fact, that he had distributed 100 rifles to Mercep's group and about 300 kilogrammes of explosives. And I also know what the whole of Yugoslavia knows and learnt from the programme that was televised later on, that Glavas did have these groups -- or, rather, Mercep had groups for silent liquidation, and that after the television programme, the man was -- the man who said all this was killed, and his name was Zvonko Ostovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I did quote that example and said that after the television programme, this man was killed. I said this before some witnesses who denied it and I'm very happy to hear this from you. I said this was a going to be a good, useful witness. Now, were these groups for secret liquidations, were they targeting the leading Serbs, communists, et cetera? Those were the criteria more or less, that they were prominent Serbs, good communists, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that -- as you say you know Glavas, by the way, is it true that he had a group of this kind that numbered 17 members and that they were all identified, while Mercep also had his own group of men and only four of those men were identified as being members of the group, and Glavas for terrorist actions, according to my information, gave Mercep 1.000 rifles and 300 kilogrammes of explosives.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't a thousand rifles, it was 100 rifles. That was our information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much explosives?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, 300 kilogrammes of explosives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You now have some details, I assume, there in front of you about that. I think they are more or less true. I can't say if there was 17 -- if Glavas had 17 members and Mercep had another number, but I do seem to recall figures of that kind, of that order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But at that time in the mid-1990 -- in mid-1990 when all the terror began and the liquidations began, there was complete peace in Yugoslavia. There were no clashes or conflicts at all at that time. Did the Serbs pose a threat to anyone at that time? Did they jeopardise anybody?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're talking about that particular period of time, that would be up until mid-1990, no, I don't know that any excessive incidents or behaviour existed at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that the terrorist group of the Croatian Uzdanica was formed at that time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Have you heard of the Croatian Uzdanica, made up of 80 men, and in Osijek 40 were under the command of Damir Horvat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That is Damir's statement to the security organs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that already in the summer of 1990 when there was complete peace, when peace reigned, that there were mass provocations that were launched and open attacks and pressure against the JNA, its members and family members, the family members of the officers?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This kind of pressure escalated as time went by, that's true, but that was from August on, or perhaps September 1990. So we had records of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. concrete acts of provocation and some JNA members were even taken into custody. And I can remember some of this. I presented this data and information when I was questioned. So I do remember this particular piece of information. From 1988 until the end of 1991, for instance, we had records for Yugoslavia as a whole. 459 attacks on members of the JNA, members and JNA facilities. Of that number, 200 took place in 1991. And 106 of those 200 took place in Croatia. So those are the facts and figures for 1991. Those are the details. As to when they started, I think that the first cases were recorded in August, August through September and later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1990, are you saying?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That would be a convenient moment to adjourn. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, before I continue, in view of the fact that it's Friday today and we're drawing close to midday, could you please ask them to give me a list of witnesses for next week, because it's high time I had it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The written list is being copied now, the letter with the names is being copied now. I think he's had advance notice of all those who are coming, in any event, on previous lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, is it true that on the 22nd of August, 1990, as early as that, 1990, in Velikovac, a MUP patrol of Croatia intercepted a military vehicle that was on assignment, a normal regular assignment, peacetime assignment, and that it searched the vehicle, mistreated the officers and soldiers, confiscated their weapons and so on?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have the concrete date and concrete event, I see. What I know is the information that I have already told you about, the attacks that started sometime in August or September. As to that particular incident, I can't quite recall it now, but as I said, I did say that the attacks started at about August. Whether that was the first incident or second, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you happen to remember another event on the 19th and 20th of September, 1990? It took place at about 2230 hours, when the MUP attacked the army vehicle, mistreated the officers, and took them into custody and took them to the MUP building. Do you happen to remember that? You must have had reports about that in view of the official function you had.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know about that event, but that did not take place in Rakici. It is Rakitje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said Rakitje.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was translated as Rakici. Anyway, the event, I know about that for certain. It involved two officers from the -- coming back from the airport, back home from the airport, and they were going behind a truck that did not have the MUP insignia to designate who it belonged to. Before the truck turned to Rakitje, which is where the MUP had its base, these two officers were intercepted and attacked, and they were taken into custody to MUP because they were suspected of having followed the vehicle, been following the vehicle, and then Boljkovac intervened to have them released, with apologies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that on the 2nd of December, 1990, in the village of Mikanovci, near Vinkovci, and that otherwise is a predominantly Serb populated village, an attempt was made to try to liquidate members of the JNA, soldiers and officers, by placing a barricade with nails on it on -- across the road in order to destroy the motor vehicles that passed by and have them turned over and have the people in them injured or killed? Do you remember that particular incident?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was December 1990, the village of Mikanovci by Vinkovci.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Vinkovci. My reports said that this took place near Vinkovci, around the barracks. I don't remember the name of the village but I do remember the incident, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was the incident as I have described it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in mid-July or, rather, the 17th of July, 1990 - so that was early on - when the JNA security organs uncovered intimations about the establishment of the illegal ZNG groups, and these were classified as secret military organisations and that the state security and the MUP of Croatia was actively involved in that.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already given you an answer to that. I said that that was linked to that competition or job vacancy announcement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that the security service following on or -- the Presidency of the SFRY uncovered and documented on the territory of Croatia precisely these paramilitary forces who were undertaking to prepare actions and that it engaged in disarming the paramilitaries in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not on assignment from the Presidency, Yugoslav state Presidency, but the Secretariat for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, there's no big difference there, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the difference was in the fact that the Presidency, the state Presidency, numbered people from the republics who precisely were engaged in these secret ongoings. So the Presidency was not informed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that on the 20th of August, 1990, Branislav Petricevic, Secretary of National Defence in Sinj, from a contingent of weapons belonging to the Territorial Defence and then purchasing these from the sport company in Split, distributed weapons to members of the HDZ in the field, and that these weapons, in the village of Otok, were issued and handed around by the local priest? Do you remember that? I'm talking about the 20th of August, 1990.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the exact date, but I think that was the material time, that's true. But before that, in Knin, local guards were organised and set up local watches by the Serbs, because there were attempts two days before that to try to disarm the police stations in Obrovac and Benkovac. And this was done by the special forces of MUP from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, why did the special unit of MUP from Zagreb disarm, go about disarming the police force, the regular, official police force in Obrovac and Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably to see that was part of the plan that existed in Croatia, as part of that plan. And that wasn't the only police station where that was done. So for -- they assessed that this was for security reasons, and they thought that these weapons could be distributed to the Serbs otherwise. But as you just mentioned the procurement of these weapons via the sport company, a work organisation in Split, the Serbs later also received weapons from the sport company of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that sport company was in Belgrade, whereas this branch in Split were their shops, their outlets. I known that Knin had an outlet of the sport company as well, and it dealt with sports, the purchase of hunting weapons legally. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you couldn't get weapons unless you had a permit to carry them, permission to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the arming I'm asking you about was illegal, unlawful, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way it was done, the quantities of weapons, objectively speaking, was illegal, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, of course. And is it true that two days prior to that -- I was asking you about the 29th of August, so on the 18th of August --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. It will take a minute or two to put right. We'll wait.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue, Mr. May? [In English] Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 18th of August, 1990, the president of the executive council of the Municipal Assembly of Split, Goran Pavlov, was working on the formation of paramilitary units from trusted cadres of the HDZ numbering 400 men called the Croatian National Guards. By then, according to information that as far as I know you had access to, he had a list of officers of the JNA in Split and the surrounding garrisons that needed to be liquidated. The unit for silent liquidations was headed by Marko Djaja, a member of the HDZ and a caterer. Is this information correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date but the information is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that in mid-August 1990, in the area of Kasteli, near Split, again a volunteer unit was formed by the HDZ? The commander was the Secretary of the National Defence in Kasteli, Kresimir Vuljak, who distributed 20 automatic rifles and several hundred pistols on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that at the beginning of October 1990, activities were started to intensively, illegally arm Croatia from abroad, specifically from Hungary, Austria, in collaboration with Slovenia, from Bulgaria, from the Brgas and Varna ports, with ships Lipa and Karolina, with planes, and it was established at the time that from Czechoslovakia twice electronic equipment was imported and a large number of pistols, only from Czechoslovakia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This must be dealt with in a way which the witness can answer. General, can you deal with the matters which are being suggested? First of all, that at the beginning of October there were activities to arm Croatia illegally, it's said, from abroad, and then a number of countries are given. So perhaps you would answer the first question: Were there such activities, to your knowledge, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there were. Only the preparations for these activities occurred earlier than October. In August already those preparations were under way. And the first -- the large contingent of weapons was discovered on the 10th -- between the 10th and 11th of October, 1991. And the data given are correct about the Lipa and the Karolina ships, only this was in January 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also correct that from Czechoslovakia alone several thousand pistols were imported, Zbrojovka? Then there was a transport from Uganda. You know the name of Kikas, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five thousand pistols were imported in two deliveries via Zagreb airport, and Kikas's plane arrived sometime in July or August 1990. No, I'm sorry, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did that plane contain?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It contained, as far as I can remember, 620 automatic rifles, Sar, a large quantity of explosives, and equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that in that period of time, the JNA, that is your organs, discovered a total of nine different channels of illegal arming of Croatia, Slovenia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Kosovo and Metohija? According to the information I have, six channels from Croatia and one each for Slovenia, and Bosnia and Kosovo and Metohija; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that as early as then, the separatists in Kosovo and Metohija were intensively being armed via Croatia and Slovenia and in the centres of Territorial Defence of Slovenia members of terrorist groups of the KLA were being trained? Not only them but others as well. And a prominent role in this was played in those days by the then secretary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Janez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One at a time. Now, the first thing is the training of groups, separatists from Kosovo, being armed, it's said, and trained in Croatia and Slovenia. Can you assist as to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can. Some corrections need to be made to this information. The security administration discovered one channel of weapons supply coming from the Kintex firm in Bulgaria towards the Albanians in Kosovo. Those were pistols that were being supplied. At the time, the KLA did not exist. There were illegal organisations in Kosovo which had their own headquarters formed in the form of Crisis Staffs, illegal Crisis Staffs for their military organisation. And a part of the Albanians in Zagreb, primarily from the cultural national club Skendija, according to a previous agreement reached with the leaders of the HDZ, were enlisting volunteers, Albanians living in the territory of Croatia. And I do not know that they went there as a compact group, but they were sent there through certain people - I know the names - and the information was that there were about 2.000 of them. Among them was a certain number of retired or demobilised officers of the JNA of Albanian ethnicity. I don't know that these activities took place in Slovenia. There were two officers there. One of them is Maljoku Naim, who was put on trial in a military tribunal. The other one's name is Demiri Fadil, who was also tried by a military tribunal in 1986. They were living in Ljubljana, and I know that, later on, they were in units of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I use the expression that these were future members of KLA terrorist groups that you have now confirmed. It is true that in those days, the KLA as such did not exist, but these were people who later cropped up again within the framework of KLA terrorist groups. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are -- you have told us even more than I mentioned, that there were about 2.000 of them that were armed and trained over there.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is the foreign connection quite clear regarding arming of Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Kosovo and Metohija? Was that part of the preparations for the break-up of Yugoslavia and its destruction?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very major conclusion. I can tell you only what I specifically know. I know of the involvement of Hungarian state organs in the delivery of weapons to Croatia in the course of 1990. And I also know of the tacit position taken by the Bulgarian authorities in those days, tacitly to tolerate export of weapons by the Kintex company to the territory of Yugoslavia. And I recall that a high-level British foreign office official had cautioned Bulgaria's diplomatic representatives in London about the information they had in connection with a ship, the Lipa, which was about to set sail. But it did set sail regardless of these comments. So I can't say that this was an international conspiracy because the British foreign office did caution the Bulgarians that the weapons would go to Croatia and that this could provoke war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have that piece of information.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that would -- it would not be correct to say the whole world or the whole of the West. I've given you just specific information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, quite specifically. Is it true that it was established that in that period, that is in mid-1990, $193 million [Realtime transcript read in error "192"] was spent on the illegal arming of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was spent, but through all those channels, that was the sum they had at their disposal, illegal funds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had information about that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had information about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that the -- at the end of 1990 and the beginning of 1991, precisely during this period of illegal intensive arming through HDZ and MUP channels, MUP opened up 18 new police poste, or stations, mainly in areas inhabited by Serbs or in ethnically mixed environments?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those stations were opened, and I think that the number you have given is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that simultaneously they broke into internal affairs secretariats where Serbs were, disarming them, seizing weapons from the reserve force of Serbs, and dismissing them from work, firing them?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this happened first and then came the formation of the stations. As far as I know, this did not happen simultaneously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what came first was the dismissal of work?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, cleansing of staff members. But you have quite a number of these questions. I don't know to what extent that is in the context of what I have been saying here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is in the context of the events you're testifying about, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've been wondering how long to leave it: All these questions are outside the scope of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A large amount of them are included in the summary that was provided, for the reasons I gave, ahead of the summary. Relevance may be extremely limited or doubtful. I don't to be seen to be, or thought even to be, a victim to what the accused might regard as favourable but there should be a limit to the degree to which he can spend his cross-examination time outside the scope of the material that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I disagree. It seems to me that what happened in Croatia prior to these events that we're dealing with may be relevant. We deal with the arming of the Serbs. It may be that the arming of the Croats is equally relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. It will be a matter for the Chamber how far, which is why I haven't interrupted, but the witness's observation is nevertheless correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's true that it goes beyond his original statement and evidence, but nonetheless, we allow relevant cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And in my view, this is relevant. Just help me with one thing, will you, General. It was put to you that the Croats had 193 million to spent on arms. I think that was the question. It wasn't stated 193 million what. Can you help us with that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. Maybe there was an error in the interpretation. I know of the figure of $192 million. Now, whether all of that money was spent on that, I don't know. I know that a certain sum that was paid to the Croats for the weapons, because the channel along which it was imported was cut and that this money stayed behind in Hungary and then it was paid back to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mentioned the figure of 192 million. Maybe there was an error Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. on the LiveNote and it appeared as 193 million, but I don't think the difference is significant. Is it true that in the Knin-Krajina, then, that is in mid-1990, a large number of armed extremists were threatening the Serbs who were scared and who started to arm themselves to defend themselves and protect their very existence?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information we had at the time, there was uncontrolled use of weapons that had been distributed. The weapons were distributed or, rather, the first contingent of automatic weapons imported from Hungary arrived in the warehouse at Mostine near Split, and it was then distributed mostly in places around Krajina. And they were discovered because they were used in an uncontrolled manner, and that is how it was known that there were armed Croats. I cannot deny that the Serbs also then, out of fear, started to get hold of hunting weapons that I mentioned.
