But I don't think that this was just an individual activity, but I think that there was some organised activity behind it, that is, to organise themselves for the defence should they be attacked. And I said I don't pretend that we had all the information available, but in those days we were monitoring the arming of Serbs, and according to that information, there were about 1.300 pieces. It is true that they returned the weapons after the Presidency issued an order in January 1991, on the 9th of January, and that they returned most of those weapons and removed the barricades. And since I'm talking about that period, it is a fact that the Croats did not return the weapons. If I'm speaking too lengthily, I can interrupt it. Up until the 19th of January, when the deadline expired for general disarmament in Croatia, the Croats returned 147 rifles out of which only 11 were Kalashnikovs from Hungary. The rest of the rifles were hunting and trophy rifles. That's all I know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go back to what you said just now. You were saying that, via Split, weapons came in for the Croatian extremists in the territory around Serb settlements, especially in Krajina. And as you said here, they irresponsibly used these weapons. Otherwise, the word that we use is Senluk, when people are just shooting for the hell of it; you show that you're armed. Was this justified, then, the fear of the Serb population there, when they saw that people were being armed around them, that they were shooting in this area, and was it justified that they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is a matter which it may be the Trial Chamber is going to have to decide, whether anybody was acting in self-defence or not. It's not a matter for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, it is for this witness to say what came before what. Was it the arming that took place first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But drawing the conclusions from that is a matter for us, not for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, is this the -- is this what happened first: When the Croats started arming themselves and when they started shooting for the hell of it, this Senluk that I referred to, and was it only then that the Serbs made an effort to procure weapons for themselves? Did the first precede the second?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite difficult for me to give a definite answer now, but what I do know definitely is that the first major organised supply of automatic weapons came in for the Croats and was distributed among the Croats from the supply that came from Hungary. In terms of timing, I think that these weapons that were obtained from the work organisation Sport, from Belgrade, came after that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's save time and let's move on. That's what I wanted to have established. Do you know that at the same time illegal arming took place when, after this import of weapons from Hungary - this was on the 11th of October, as you said - the first quantity arrived in Mostine, the warehouse of Mostine, with MGV automatic rifles on the 22nd of October from the Slovenian company Gorenje, and that a certain Djaja took over these weapons, who took over part of the weapons and also equipment for diversions and sabotages. You had information about that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about a certain quantity of MGVs from Maribor, and this piece of information is correct about taking over part of the arms and equipment, actually that Djaja did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the session of the Presidency of the SFRY for which information was provided and it is proof of illegal arming in Croatia, and this information came from your service or, rather, from the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, the session was not held then because Vasil Tupurkovski was absent. However, Mesic took this piece of information to Croatia where they were shocked about the fact that the JNA knew about this.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is known. However, this is a situation when the then president, Borisav Jovic, presided over the Presidency, this piece of information, because it was very confidential, was not distributed before the session, but during the session itself Mr. Jovic did give this piece of information to the members of the Presidency, but then he did not discuss this as a separate item on the agenda. Then the next regular session of the Presidency was supposed to be held only on the 9th of January. The effects of that could have been disastrous. The man who was working on discovering this channel was in jeopardy. But there's another interesting aspect to all of this. When they received this information, and I think that they got it the same evening through Mr. Mesic who went to Zagreb the same evening, then they tried to withdraw the weapons that they had distributed through the HDZ. However, since nobody wanted to return the weapons, we in the security administration said that they actually carried out a manoeuvre with these weapons. They printed over 50.000 IDs for the reserve force of the MUP and then distributed these IDs to members of the HDZ so that they could justify the fact that they had weapons in their possession. I feel it is my duty to say that, later on, the federal MUP carried out their own checks and investigations and realised that many improper things had been going on, and the Federal Secretary of the Interior, Mr. Gracanin, had been informed about this. However, this information was not made public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the consequence of this discovery, namely that there was illegal arming, was the fictitious legalisation that took place. I have the information here that 54.000 IDs were printed of the reserve police force for Croatia, and that is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said 50.000, but possibly it is 54.000. But I said 50.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, that was the way in which weapons were not returned, but they remained in their hands?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only that. That is how the fact was concealed that through the HDZ a paramilitary arming was being founded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that undeniable, that through the HDZ a paramilitary army was being formed?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is undeniable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when the Presidency passed a decision to disarm all paramilitary formations, the Croatian formations returned only 157 pieces, and out of them, only 11 Kalashnikovs.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said only -- I said 147.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But all of it was just old iron except for the 11 Kalashnikovs; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But Mr. Mesic said in the Presidency that the deadline for returning weapons should be extended for another 48 hours. That was on the 19th of January. On the same evening, we received information which was checked out, documented, and it was on television, that Minister Spegelj passed a decision to the effect that weapons would not be returned. Rather, the entire force should be placed on a state of alert and military facilities should be blocked. Specifically what I know, because I was then in Virovitica, it was the barracks in Virovitica that was blocked. The soldiers who tried to go for medical check-ups to Zagreb were arrested by these armed civilians around the barracks, and it is only after that that tensions went down at the intervention of the Presidency and the federal authorities, because after that, the army had also raised its own state of alert. That is what I know about this particular event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this increase in tensions is only a consequence of the fact that decisions of the Presidency were not carried out, the fact that weapons were retained, weapons were not returned, weapons that the paramilitary formations used for their own armament.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot draw any conclusions. I'm just presenting the facts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that Serbs who had bought some -- some hunting rifles and pistols through the Sport work organisation had returned their weapons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that they returned them in part. However, Serbs had some automatic weapons. Because Mr. Martic, already I think on the 18th or 19th of August, 1990, when the MUP tried to break into the police stations in Obrovac and Benkovac, distributed the weapons of the reserve force of the MUP to the reserve force of the MUP and probably to others who volunteered. So as far as I know, it was about 100 automatic rifles and machine-guns, I'm not aware of the exact figures, but they also had a certain quantity of automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But when the Presidency issued an order to disarm, the Serbs returned their weapons and the Croat side did not.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that all the automatic rifles were returned but not all the hunting guns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking about the hunting guns. And do you remember that Mesic had requested for delaying the deadline for another 48 hours because they had been warned that the army would react if they did not comply with the decision of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that instead of returning weapons, they carried out mobilisation then?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the Serbs were convinced - I mean they returned their weapons - that the Croats would return their weapons too and that the decision of the Presidency would be complied with?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what they were convinced of, but I know that they accepted this order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that then on the basis of what was known and on the basis of all the checks that were made as to whether everything had been returned, that at that time in the Knin Krajina there were very few weapons, a bit over a hundred rifles and three machine-guns? Is that correct? Because the Serbs were convinced that everybody would return their weapons and that's why they returned theirs too.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers to the automatic weapons of the police station that was returned, and I already said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So can we say that in accordance with the decision of the Presidency, the Serbs returned their weapons? According to the Vance Plan, Serbs returned their weapons again, so two times they returned their weapons. And here, when Kirudja was a witness, we established that it was only after the attack on Maslenica in January 1993 that they took weapons again because UNPROFOR did not protect them. So two times they returned weapons, and is that what you know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This witness doesn't know what any other witness said. It's no good asking about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that they returned weapons the other time, when UNPROFOR came?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that these weapons were put under international control. They were stored and put under international control. As for these other comments, I cannot deal with that. So I have given these facts and figures, and there is no need for me to repeat them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember, for example, that the Serbs in Krajina, then, would sell a cow, for instance, to buy a rifle because they felt threatened?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such cases. Two cows had to be sold for one rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct -- you mentioned this ship Lipa. This is the 31st of December, 1990. Seventy tonnes of weapons came in through Varna in eight containers. That's how they were delivered.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the figure of eight containers. I do not remember the weight in tonnes. I remember the company that was involved in the transport. It was called Zagrebtrans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that all of this was declared as whisky and cigarettes that were being transferred to the island of Krk? And according to the customs declaration, the ship was supposed to sail to the port of Bizerta [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the operative information that we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the then president of Croatia, Tudjman, after the film about Spegelj and the illegal armament was televised, firmly promised the Presidency of the SFRY that all paramilitary formations would be disarmed and that the perpetrators would be punished?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I was in Zagreb, and that is what I was told by the security administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that is not what was actually done.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that on the 26th of January, he made a statement similar to what you said just now. He made a public statement. However, as far as I know, a day later he went to Austria for consultations, and after that when he returned, he changed his decision. He said that the HDZ was not being armed, rather, it was the MUP of Croatia that was being armed, that Croatia was entitled to that, and that the Yugo army would not be in a position to arrest Croatian citizens. And then the district attorney, the district prosecutor in Bjelovar initiated criminal proceedings against me because of the allegedly unauthorised arrest of civilians in Croatia, and that is when I became a wanted man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did Tudjman meet with in Austria?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. Somebody from the top Austrian leadership.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that after this promise was made and then when he changed his position after receiving instructions in Austria, Zarko Domljan, a high official of the HDZ, I think he was even president of the Croatian parliament for a while, at the session of this Central Committee of the HDZ in Zagreb, he said that the attempt to disarm Croatia was the last blow to the independence of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that. He's not the only one who said that. After this campaign, after the 27th of January, this was a widespread campaign, and that is the way it was carried out, in that spirit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you happen to remember that at the time there was talk about intensifying links with Slovenia, for example, as well as Bosnia-Herzegovina, Macedonia, and the leaders of Kosovo Albanians in order to exert pressure on the Serbs and pressure to break up Yugoslavia? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That took place before the matters we're discussing now, and I know that there were contacts with Mr. Rugova, for example, and I also know about the contacts between Spegelj and Fikret Abdic. And after importing weapons from Hungary, he offered a certain quantity of weaponry in order to arm the Muslims over there. And also, he was in contact with Rugova with respect to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that Marko Nobilo, Tudjman's advisor, after the film on Spegelj was shown on the 31st of January, said that the Croatian leadership had finally come to realise that Croatia had no prospects for the future within the SFRY and that that is why Tudjman had many contacts with Western representatives who gave him support for secession? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were operative data along those lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as you are the best placed person to answer my next question, let me first of all start off by saying that we had here, sitting in the seat you're sitting in now, people who challenged the Spegelj film.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I've told you before that there's no point putting to this witness what other witnesses said. What he can give is his own evidence. Now, I've no doubt you're going to invite him to comment on what other witnesses have said. That is not a proper question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Fine. Then I'll ask him directly and ask him what he knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the film about Spegelj fabricated? Was it a false film, a falsified film, a forgery, or was it authentic and correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the material shown in the film, and I'm now talking about the material that was secretly filmed by the military security service, and I state categorically that they are absolutely authentic. Now, in uncovering the illegal importation of weapons, 19 and a half hours of television footage, secret footage, was recorded, was filmed, and a very small portion was incorporated into that particular film and there was about 120 hours of phonic recording, voice, audio recording. So I state that the material is authentic, the film is authentic, judging by the material it showed. As to the way it was mounted and where the public statements were taken from and how these were placed parallelly or mounted, montage was made with the filming, it wasn't that lies were mounted, but it was based on the truth. That is what I know about. The editing was done in that way. And there were different statements from January 1991 when the film first saw the light of day, about Spegelj who, at the time, completely denied the authenticity of anything that was shown and everything that was shown. And then the third man that took part in the programme, Perisic was his name from the Croatian MUP, he gave an assessment and he said that according to his knowledge, to the best of his knowledge, the material that was shown was indeed authentic. So from this categoric denial in the month of January, later on Minister Spegelj acknowledged that he was not fully aware and had allowed this man to take the films he took. He was not cautious enough. And as to the film The Death of Yugoslavia, I think Perica Juric commented on that and commented on that film.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. I want to clarify the answer, if the general would. You're saying that the footage in the film is authentic. You can say that because it comes from the military security service. But what I didn't quite follow was what you were saying about the editing. You said something to the effect as to where it was mounted and where the public statements were taken from, and you made some comment about that which I don't follow. Now, it may be that you didn't wish to comment on the editing, but if you do, could you clarify what you meant when talking about as to the way it was mounted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. Well, perhaps I gave an incomplete answer here because of the time constraints. I didn't want to take away the accused's time. Let me repeat. The material that was shown in the film as secret filming done by the security organs are absolutely authentic, and I took part directly in the operations of having this secretly filmed, in the secret filming. Which means that I didn't get it from any other security organ, I organised these operations directly and took part in that secret filming. And this raw material I personally took to Belgrade to the Federal Secretary for National Defence. And that material, once again, I returned -- after it was shown and seen, I returned it to me in Zagreb. And nobody could fabricate it or rig it in any way. So that is the first point as to the authenticity of the material. I say that I am responsible for the authenticity of the material. The material was kept and stored in the security service if some harm hasn't come to them now. Now, I spoke about the montage of the film and how it was edited and mounted. The editing of the film, or montage, is a professional term used when a film is actually made and it consists of different sequences. And when you direct a film, you have to decide upon the sequence and -- of the elements that you're going to play and show in order to show something. The term "editing" in the technical sense of the word means combining, compiling what was publicly stated at meetings in the Croatian parliament or statements made over Croatian television and things of that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. sort by individual top leaders from Franjo Tudjman via Spegelj and others. So they made statements. They said, "We did not arm the HDZ," for example. And then they would play parts of the secret filming, the secret footing where Spegelj actually speaks and says that the HDZ was indeed being armed. And then Minister Boljkovac cautions him, warns him and said this should not have gone through the HDZ but that everything should have come under the MUP. And then you would have another sequence played from another public statement that had been made, for example, and then once again, the secret footage would be played, what these people were actually saying tete-a-tete, when they were sitting alone together. So it wasn't montage and editing in the sense of producing something that was untrue; it was the way in which these sequences were made and confronting the public statements of these individuals with what they were doing in private, secretly. I don't know if that makes it clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Yes. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's make this question simple, General, simplify matters. You yourself said you didn't get this secondhand but that you organised it all yourself personally in the official capacity you occupied, and as you saw the film that was shown to the public, publicly, was that film completely true and truthful?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true and correct that Spegelj, on the occasion, said, "Our absolute concept is to have all the officers killed, if necessary on their thresholds, because for an open conflict with the JNA, we still do not have enough power and strength to do so," that that was the gist and the approach that they had at that particular time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't confirm whether those are the exact words he uttered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's allow that it was a paraphrase.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You needn't read it as an exact quotation.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he organised preparations for the officers through whom I obtained that information, who were Croats, by the way, and that they should prevent officers, when the sound -- the alarm is sounded, that they would be able to get to the barracks, that they should be liquidated on their own doorsteps. And as to the cautions and warnings of officers of how people -- how they expected people to be killed in front of their own homes, he said that nothing should be asked, no questions should be asked, that everything should be cut down -- and I'm now saying the exact words. He used the verb "sisati," that no questions should be asked whether they were men or women, everyone must be cut down, mowed down. So those were the exact words. The second part is this: Of the less senior officers who were arrested, one of them was brought to trial, the NCOs, and they endeavoured to form a group who would, in the barracks when he gave the signal, liquidate the officer on duty, the duty officer in the barracks, disarm the guards and lock up, he said, all Serbs in the cellars. Lock all the Serbs up in the cellars. Give them a glass of water to -- as for the Albanians and Muslims, give them five bullets each and let them go home, those of them who wished to go home. And the second NCO, who was also brought to trial, he prepared him to disarm the border huts, the frontier huts that they worked in and to take the weapons and distribute them to the Croatians in the surrounding villages. So this -- these were film -- this was footage that we first got -- we first got the audio tape. And they were taken on the 14th of October 1990, the audio recordings, and Minister Boljkovac was present. And they moved around in his car, they drove in his car. And then I was given the task of taking television footage after the audio recordings. And that's when most of the material was taken and most of the filming done. For purposes of having the whole truth come out, it is my duty to state the following: Already on the 22nd or the 23rd of October, 1990, those first original television films were seen also by Mr. Jovic in General Kadijevic's cabinet or offices. So he was informed already in the second half of October. He was shown that footage and the material. Not to be too lengthy, but let me say that I had occasion when I met Mr. Jovic to ask him why Spegelj had not been arrested, because I was later blamed for the fact that he had not been arrested. In fact, this was a decision taken by the Presidency itself, that the proceedings against Spegelj would follow regular legal court procedure. That is to say that he would be invited, summoned, he would be -- he would respond. If he did not respond, then a warrant would be put out for his arrest. And when I asked Mr. Jovic why Spegelj had not in fact been arrested, his answer was, "Well, what would have changed had we arrested him?" So that was his answer. "How would that have changed things?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how, then, do you explain, please, tell me this, because quite obviously there's some very interesting events and details coming out here now: If you had at your disposal what the Federal Secretary Kadijevic had at his disposal, and the president of the Yugoslav state Presidency Jovic, if they already had that material in October, how is it then possible that the problem about disarmament and information explaining and expounding the proposal to disarm these formations should come up before the Presidency only in December, as late as December? Because that was two months later.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's one thing to have initial data and information, and it's quite another thing to have dealt with the problem in its entirety. So parallel armament did not take place only in the Virovitica and Podravina regions. I presented information about the distribution of weapons via the warehouses in Mostine, for example. In order to arrest somebody, to arrest those who were responsible for that, what was provided for was -- that is to say, almost 40 people were involved and their arrest. From the Vujak that you mentioned, this man Vujak, via other people, the president of the executive council of the Split municipality, for example, and this whole operation was being prepared for the 3rd and 4th of December, 1990, between the 3rd and 4th of December, 1990. And then it was put off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, why didn't you arrest them all?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can ask Mr. Jovic that, not me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, was it Jovic's business and duty to order the arrest of these presidents of the executive councils or whatever? What was that man's name, the man you mentioned or the man I mentioned? I can't remember. You've just said I mentioned his name. Was that the duty of the president of the Yugoslav state Presidency or the security organs who establish -- who have established that people were being armed illegally, that weapons were being brought in and that the integrity of the country, the constitutional order of the country was being jeopardised? To implement the law, do you need a Yugoslav state Presidency president decision?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this case, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I must say I don't follow you there. I don't understand why. All right. Tell me, as you've just mentioned -- or, rather, let's go a step back. We have observed, and I think I've noted this down, so far in the meantime, having moved on from the generalities, I asked you about 60 questions and you gave affirmative answers to practically all of them, and that other side over there reacted, they said did they have direct links. Now, if we bear in mind everything that was happening over there, we mentioned Glavas and the detachments for silent liquidation, the killings of Serbs, shooting in Kninska Krajina, the arming that took place before the Serbs had armed themselves, the fact that they were in jeopardy, their lives were under threat and all the other things that took place, is it quite clear that it was an armed, violent secession on the part of Croatia seceding from Yugoslavia, contrary to the constitution? It was armed, it was violent, it was an armed, violent act of secession and it was being prepared --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think this is a matter which the Trial Chamber may ultimately have to determine. It sounds like a mixed matter of fact and law. What you can do is to ask the witness what he understood of the situation, what did the situation that he was dealing with appear like to him. You can ask him that, if you want.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, if I'm asking a general, General Aleksandar Vasiljevic, then I expect an answer conveying his position, nobody else's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I told you it was not a proper question. It was a matter of fact and law for the Trial Chamber to determine. Let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, was this for you as a JNA general an obvious armed secession on the part of Croatia from Yugoslavia and an attack on Yugoslavia and its institutions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I've ruled against you. General, you can deal with it in this way: From your own experience and your own knowledge, how did the JNA react to this situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I say first that all the persons who were arrested and put on trial before the military Tribunal in Zagreb in the first half of 1991 were found guilty of the criminal act of armed rebellion, according to the constitutional order in force at the time. That's one thing. And according to the impression that I had - and that is why I did the job I did, risking a great deal as did the other people working on it - we felt that preparations were under way for a violent secession of Croatia from Yugoslavia. And there were many indicators. Not only those that were shown here, but also when the conflict broke out in Slovenia, when Tudjman called Alija Izetbegovic to call on all Bosniak soldiers and officers to abandon the JNA, his aim was for the armed conflict which had been under preparation against the JNA in Croatia to be -- to spread to Bosnia and Macedonia. And we called this in the army as the opening of the southern front. And two of his advisors were sent, one to Sarajevo and another to Skopje. If necessary, I can give you the names of these people. We were convinced that we could successfully defend Yugoslavia if all these formations were disarmed, regardless of the ethnicity of the people carrying those weapons. However, at a meeting of the Presidency held in March, such a decision was not supported. And this was followed, first of all, by attacks on the JNA, and I am aware of official correspondence from the MUP of Croatia that, in future, the JNA should no longer be referred to as the Yugoslav People's Army but as the "occupying army." And as this is a good opportunity, let me inform you of the following: Out of more than 2.700 arrested members of the JNA in Croatia, 85 per cent were captured in their barracks, 15 per cent in their apartments, and almost no one in open spaces or in conflict. The policy was, as they said, that the army should remain in the barracks. Those barracks were blocked, and people were killed inside them. In Bjelovar, my security officer was killed, Captain Jovanovic, who also worked on the discovery of channels for the delivery of weapons. He and his commander, Colonel Kovacevic, and Lieutenant Colonel Vasic, the assistant for morale, they were stripped to the waist and liquidated in front of a line-up of soldiers. I have TV footage about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It may not seem very important just now, but it could prove to be important later on. Let me ask you one more thing, which doesn't appear to be very significant. Do you remember that there were certain excuses given regarding the illegal purchase of weapons to the effect that the SSNO did not allow -- that is, the Federal Defence Ministry, did not allow the MUP of Croatia to purchase weapons in our own domestic factory, that is the Crvena Zastava factory. My question is, is it true that the Federal Ministry of Defence did not refuse to allow the MUP of Croatia to purchase weapons from Crvena Zastava as requested, as claimed by Spegelj, but that Spegelj, on the 5th of October in Hungary contracted purchase of weapons before he had received an answer from the federal secretariat about purchase from Crvena Zastava and that the federal ministry did not veto the Croatian request but responded that it should be selective, that a certain amount could be purchased straight away and another contingent would be manufactured next year because the federal secretariat, in those days, believed that these were regular supplies for the police, renewal of the weaponry, et cetera? So even that excuse was not truthful.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that the response sent to Croatia arrived in due time, that is, within the fixed one-month period envisaged. And the reply contained what you said. It was addressed on the 10th of October. According to documents we had, Spegelj, five days before that, that is on the 5th of October, he was already in Hungary with Zdravko Mrksic, who was then Minister of Foreign Affairs of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that as soon as Spegelj took over his duty as a minister, was radical in his demands for attacking barracks, disarming of the army, liquidating officers and their families, breaking in with sabotage groups into military facilities to liquidate guards and security officers, and that even Tudjman did not agree to this and he complained of Tudjman's hesitation?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, and he wrote that in his book Memories of a Soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned he offered weapons to Fikret Abdic, of whom he said that he was petrified and refused it, because -- I think this to be probable, because Abdic was not the kind of man who was prone to any kind of bloodshed. Then he offered weapons to Rugova. He asked that the Albanians in Kosovo start an armed rebellion straight away, and so on. Did you have information about all this?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've already testified about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That would be a convenient moment. We will adjourn now. It's the time. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've spoken to the witness on --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could we have private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm just going to deal with one other administrative matter it may be convenient to deal with now before we continue the cross-examination. I referred earlier this week to the application to admit the 64 statements under Rule 92 bis, and we have been thinking of the most convenient way of dealing with this by way of argument, and we propose to deal first with those statements to which the amici have made observations which put them in a different category really from the others, and those are B-1732, C-1201, C-1231, C-1150, C-1090. We will find a time next week convenient to hear some argument upon those particular statements and then we'll deal with the others probably portion by portion. It may be convenient - I don't know what anybody thinks about this - to deal with them by way of location. Perhaps this is not the right moment to discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I -- thank you for that. Can I confirm that the queries you raised about witnesses whose material have not be disclosed can be answered shortly; it now has all been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If it cannot be Monday, because Monday is a day I can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will avoid Monday. We will be continuing the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. General, sorry to have detained you for that. Yes, Mr. Milosevic, if you'd like to go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you mentioned a session of the Presidency of the SFRY held in March 1991. Do you remember that a proposal was made there to introduce measures of emergency precisely because of what you said, namely, Croatia's non-compliance with regard to weapons and the disbanding of paramilitary formations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that then at the session of the Presidency the vote was 4 to 3 in favour of adopting emergency measures, but they were not adopted only because Drnovsek was not present at the session. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the arming of Serbs in Croatia actually intensified only after that session of the Presidency of Yugoslavia? That was the 12th of March, 1991, when the proposal of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence to introduce emergency measures was reduced and also when the decision of the Presidency to disband paramilitary units in the SFRY did not come through?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no specific knowledge as to the extent of arming. I cannot give reliable figures on that. But by way of a general conclusion, it is right that after that, they started organising themselves, that roadblocks were set up once again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After these attempts failed to disarm those who were threatening them?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the March session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Is it true that Tudjman then talked with Izetbegovic in order to open a corridor so that deserters could pass unhindered, primarily deserters from the JNA, and in order to reach concrete agreement, he sent his representatives to Bosnia-Herzegovina and also met with Rugova; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know about the fact that he sent his representatives to Macedonia and Sarajevo. This was primarily for the sake of coordination of activities that were to be carried out in these two republics. According to a similar recipe, they were supposed to be engaged in this same process of secession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can one then state that this was their mutual agreement on mutual military cooperation for the purposes of secession?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was Tudjman's endeavour, to reach this kind of agreement, but I think in Macedonia this process had not started, inter alia, because we managed to have the cooperation of the Ministry of the Interior of Macedonia who recognised the jurisdiction of the federal MUP. This process had been delayed for a while in Bosnia-Herzegovina also because of the cooperation of the then Minister of the Interior, Alija Delimustafic. However, later on, from March onwards, this process would move in a different direction because the Patriotic League of Peoples, as a paramilitary formation of the Party of Democratic Action, the SDA, had already started taking actions of their own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Party of Democratic Action is Izetbegovic's party; right? And this Patriotic League of Peoples worked as a terrorist organisation practically, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not use that word, "terrorist." I think that the right word is "paramilitary organisation," which had in its plans some such activities as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "such," you mean terrorist?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean special units, diversionary units that were established for such activities. Their use had to be verified by the military Crisis Staff of the Patriotic League in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, do you remember the particular piece of information that there were four or five diversion sabotage groups that in the period from 1991 until the beginning of January 1992 were discovered? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I remember the most characteristic part when an attempt was made to blow up a military train at the railway station in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, in Brcko. And this group in the territory of Brcko, where had it been brought in from? Is it true that it was brought in from Croatia precisely to carry out this attack against military facilities at the railway station in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were caught at the bridge on the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Is it correct that another group was in the territory of Vojvodina and that it was also brought in from Croatia and that it consisted of 17 members and that they then tried to get into the military barracks in Sombor?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, but this happened later, when broader operations started in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that a third group was caught, those who were trying to blow up the bridge between Montenegro and Bosnia-Herzegovina at Scepan Polje?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This group was not captured. Information was revealed about that. This was given to the Ministry of Interior of Montenegro and to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is why reinforced security was requested for that particular bridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that two brothers, members of the diversionary group caught in Bosanski Samac when they were transporting weapons and equipment for 100 men in Listica? Is that correct? Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. These are the Kovac brothers, but this is not a diversionary group. The two of them did carry out illegal transports of complete equipment for 100 men. They were captured in Bosanski Samac, I think, or in Bosanski Brod, at those checkpoints that were shared by the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, one can put it this way, there was cooperation between the JNA and the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina in order to prevent illegal weapons flows; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that in the same period several channels and groups were discovered that were trying to import weapons into Croatia from all over the world? And do you know who the immediate perpetrators of illegal arms imports were? In addition to Hungary, arms were imported from Italy and Great Britain as well.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security administration worked on something which was called -- the code name was Kanal, "channel." This operatively covered a large contingent of weapons in the port of Constanza in Romania. These were weapons that had belonged to the PLO while Ceaucescu was in power. And it is correct that emissaries from Croatia tried to import those weapons. This is the period from the 6th of August onwards. Actually, 6th of August, 1991. That's when I became aware of this. And then through these operative positions, an effort was made for them not to take land routes, because later on, objectively, the border with Hungary was not under JNA control. The following combination was made; that the weapons had to be transported by ship for security reasons, and then two shiploads of weapons -- and I know that in one there were over 50.000 Kalashnikovs, but then there were also heavier weapons, like artillery guns and artillery pieces. This import was being delayed in order to find a forwarder. So then the weapons were unloaded, probably because of this risk of war, and somebody had to pay for the insurance, et cetera, et cetera. So to make a long story short, these were two shiploads from Constanza, and while I was in active service, these ships actually never left Constanza going to Croatia, and the weapons didn't either. However, the money had been paid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know anything about the import of weapons from Italy and Great Britain?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for sure about weapons from Italy, and I was in contact with the head of the Italian intelligence service, General Ramponni in Belgrade. We gave information about that channel, and in Genoa, after that, the Italian police arrested five Croat arms traders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know anything about Great Britain?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I told you about Great Britain, that the British foreign office reacted to information about the ship of Lipa, and they cautioned the Bulgarian embassy in London that it would not be good for peace in the territory of Yugoslavia for these weapons to be found in that area. So that is the piece of information that I am aware of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that on the 5th of May, 1991, Tudjman had a meeting in Trogir with the top people of the HDZ and with the authorities from the Dalmatian municipalities where he presented the following assessment; that the JNA was jeopardising Croatian democracy, that something should have been done earlier but it wasn't too late even then but that there should be a protest rally in front of the building of the naval district and also in Split and that at least 5.000 people should be engaged in blocking the JNA in the naval district and that is the only way in which the JNA could be compelled to act differently. Did you have this information?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did. I am not aware of this figure that he mentioned, this figure of 5.000 people. Actually, he was answering questions there as to why the Croatian leadership did not do anything in order to discipline the JNA. That's the way they had put it. And he said quite literally, "Don't ask me to do that. Get together. Go out tomorrow and block the command headquarters of the military naval district and do it that way." And then he also said through the independent trade unions in Split - and Jure Sundov was their president, I believe - a big rally was organised, the command headquarters was blocked, actually, and that is when an armed attack took place against the command, and the military police that was providing security there in an armoured transporter, that is when the soldier Gesovski was killed, and then Lieutenant Egeric was wounded. And another soldier who was in the armoured vehicle was almost strangled, but then they finally managed to close the turret and to pull him in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let's be very precise about this. This meeting in Trogir where Tudjman suggested to them that they should rally together, this was on the 5th of May. And already on the next day, the 6th of May, the rally did take place, and these members of the JNA were killed in front of the command of the military naval district; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the Yugoslav flag was taken down from the flag mast and the flag with the chequerboard was put up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And is it true that after that it was precisely the MUP of Croatia that, in order to protect the organisers of this action, hid the -- hid Jure Sundov and also the two policemen who took part in this crime as well as other people who were known to have illegally taken weapons?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know about Jure Sundov and about the two policemen that had killed and wounded members of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, is it correct -- is it correct, this piece of information that I have here, that you or, rather, the security administration of the army mediated in the exchange of Ivan Duspara, Mate Sabljic, Branko Glavinic, and Ronald Zvonaric? These are people from Split who strangled the soldier in Split; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not mediate in that exchange. That exchange was carried out according to the decision taken by the federal secretary. In that exchange, Kikas was exchanged as well. He's a citizen of Canada, and he took part in the import of weapons with this Boeing aeroplane from Uganda. At that time, General Aksentijevic was exchanged, who had been arrested by members of the Croatian MUP at the entrance into Zagreb, and also seven other officers. And at that time, 19 arrested security officers in Croatia were exchanged, and seven pilots who had been gunned down. So that was a total of 34 members of the army headed by General Aksentijevic who were exchanged for this so-called group of the Split stranglers who were already taken out of JNA jurisdiction and who were sent to the penitentiary in Foca, to serve their terms there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of what they had committed, were these persons who could have been considered prisoners of war? Just give me a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is what I think too. Since they were not prisoners of war, how was it possible that they were exchanged for captured JNA members in the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had the position taken by the Federal Secretary for National Defence that all captured members of the National Guards Corps could be exchanged for only one arrested or imprisoned member of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I understand it, top priority was given to care for the security of JNA members, and that was the reason for this.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did a delegation or representative of the Red Cross attend these exchanges, as prescribed, especially the one in Zagreb when you handed over Kikas and the others?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A man was present on behalf of the Croatian authorities, as far as I know, a representative of the Jewish community in Zagreb. And I don't -- I'm not sure that members of the Red Cross were present. I can't remember that. I do know that there were problems in carrying out the exchange, because a lieutenant security officer from Gospic, his name was Ivan Duspara, they didn't bring him to the exchange, and I didn't want to agree to the exchange without him. The reason why he wasn't brought for the exchange was that, after being brought out of the prison in Gospic twice, the persons escorting him pretended to execute him twice. Like a fake execution was carried out, but as he survived and didn't have a heart attack, they beat him up in a catering establishment close to Zagreb. And as he was all black and blue from the beatings, they didn't dare hand him over until he recovered a little. And then we received him two days later, while he still had visible traces of the beatings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move away from these events in Split now and the background to those events which I hope we have established accurately now. Is it true that on the 24th and 25th of July, 1991 near Suho Polje, which is on the road between Podravska Slatina and Virovitica, a military vehicle was stopped by the National Guards Corps, fire was opened at it when a Major Radoslav Vuckovic, the commander of the frontier battalion, and another two soldiers were seriously injured? Do you remember that event?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, because I knew Vuckovic personally while I was working in Virovitica. With his patrol he removed warrant posters issued against me, and I think that was one of the reasons he was attacked. He was seriously wounded and transferred later to the JNA -- to the medical academy. When he recovered, he was assigned to the Uzice Corps. And then, being a commander, he was killed by a drunken reservist in front of other soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that on that same day, around 2200 hours, 300 metres from the barracks in Vinkovci, at a checkpoint put up by members of the MUP of Croatia, without any reason or cause, Goran Mihajlovic was killed and Boban Kalimancevic, both sergeants, and though the perpetrators were identified, they remained unpunished and suffered no consequences?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, that these two non-commissioned officers were killed, and it is also true that in those days, in Vinkovci, like a wax model of the head of the commander had been made, who was still alive. But this wax head was put on a pole and carried around the barracks to cause a psychosis of insecurity. And this -- the name of the staff sergeant was Kalimancevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, but you didn't tell me whether you know that the perpetrators were identified and were not punished.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And is it true that on the 25th of July, half an hour after midnight, an armed attack was carried out by the MUP of Croatia against the military units securing the bridge at Bogojevo

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know of that event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that on the 18th of September, a terrorist group of the Croatian army attacked a military column in Studena Vrela, near Listica, when a sergeant, Vojko Ceh, was killed, as well as a soldier, whereas on the side of the attackers Ludvig Pavlovic was killed, who was a member of an Ustasha terrorist organisation and a member of a terrorist group which in 1972 had been infiltrated and executed at Radusa in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but he survived that execution, and an ID card was found on him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're getting a long way from this in a huge amount of detail. Deal with events in 1991. Was there this incident, General, when a sergeant and -- was killed on the 18th of September? Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. He was a non-commissioned officer of the military police, a Slovene by ethnicity. Ludvig Pavlovic was released. He was amnestied by Mr. Mesic when he became president of the Presidency. He was set free and immediately after that, he joined the Croatian armed forces in Western Herzegovina and that is where he was killed. And it is true that an official ID was found on him of the MUP of Croatia. This is an example that I told Mr. Alija Izetbegovic about on the 5th of February, 1992, and a subsequent event when another officer was kidnapped, that is captain and pilot Dragan Stojcinovic in Mostar. And Alija Izetbegovic told me on that occasion, "Leave Western Herzegovina alone. It was never part of Bosnia." So he was rather indifferent to this because there were many excesses in Western Herzegovina which, in my judgement, if I'm entitled to make one now, was treated as a component part of Croatia. And this didn't seem to bother the president who was in power at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this during the time when there was an agreement between Tudjman and Izetbegovic and the Slovenian leadership and these others that we mentioned, the emissaries who went to Macedonia and Kosovo and so on, that their cadres should abandon the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tudjman's first appeal to Izetbegovic to call on Bosniak members to walk out of the JNA was made on the 30th of June in 1991. That is the fourth or third day after the conflict started in Slovenia. And I can't say that it accepted it. In other words, I don't know that there was any agreement on some sort of an alliance modelled on what the -- what Croatia and Slovenia did. But I do know that at a session of the federal council for the protection of the constitutional order, after we presented all this information as to what was going on in Western Herzegovina, Mr. Izetbegovic was advised to send a Demos to Tudjman, a protest reacting to this and also to the fact that the territory of Neum municipality, which belongs to Bosnia-Herzegovina, was being used for the transfer of National Guards Corps forces from Metkovic, that is Western Herzegovina, towards Dubrovnik. I know that he didn't wish to accept to make such a demos, although it was proposed by the federal council for the protection of the constitutional order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had that proposal been accepted, would it have reduced tension and removed the threat of conflicts in that area?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not. I think that things had already gone too far by then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're saying that this was sometime in mid-1991, when without any doubt Slovene cadres, following instructions from their leadership, and Croatian cadres upon instruction from their leadership, were leaving the JNA as of the mid-1991.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a major campaign according to the -- of the break-up of the JNA along ethnic seams or lines. That was the expression used. I think that that was not true, and I have given information about the air force specifically, as to the large percentage of officers who were not Serbs or Montenegrins. That campaign was spread intentionally, and the JNA was not abandoned in Bosnia and Herzegovina with the withdrawal of Muslims from the JNA. I think that a large number of those people believed in Yugoslavia, and it was only at the end, at the end of this entire process, when the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was constituted, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. when the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised, there were few people who deserted from the JNA. They realised where this was heading, they submitted legal requests, and left the army. But this could be said of March and April 1992 in particular. This applies to that period. Many of them remained honourable officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know, I assume, though then you were already retired, that a large number of Muslims, so let's talk about the area of Bijeljina, for instance, or Derventa and so on, that they were within the ranks of the army of Republika Srpska and were defending it, together with the Serbs, from Muslim extremists. They were defending their towns and villages.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's an idealised presentation of the events. Unfortunately, there were some ugly scenes and events too. I had an officer, a colonel who was a Muslim, who was chief of security in Ljubljana and who withdrew together with his troops to Bosnia, and his wife who was a Slovene, committed suicide by setting fire to herself. He suffered from a heart attack as a result, and he couldn't even attend her funeral. When the war in Bosnia started, he was still on sick leave in the place of his birth, somewhere near Bosanski Novi, I'm not quite sure about that right now. The Serbs held him under blockade there. He was under a kind of curfew when he would be allowed to leave his house to buy something. His house was not destroyed. He managed to get to Germany, and he was in a camp, a refugee camp there, and that is where he died. And he's a terrible example of the fate of some honourable officers. And what the climate had -- was like that had swept the area at the time. The Serbs who should have helped him. And I appealed to some officers that I knew to take care of him. He survived, that's true, but he was under blockade, and that is true. Under a kind of house arrest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are many such tragic individual examples, but let us try to establish one thing: As you were speaking about illegal arming and about the distribution of weapons, particularly in areas surrounding the Serbs, and incidents in ethnically mixed environments, is it true that on the other hand, in units of the TO formed by local Serbs there were also Croats who wanted to defend the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the movement of the League of Communists for Yugoslavia had animated its members, and the members of that party were multi-ethnic, and they were encouraging people to join the JNA. They didn't join as an organised group, nor did they have any party or ideological insignia. And in that sense, I can confirm that there were Croats and Muslims, communists, in particular, who joined the JNA. What happened to them later when the army of Republika Srpska was formed, I don't know. I know for the period while the JNA still existed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of the case of a brigade headed by a Muslim in the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But we'll come back to that later. Do you remember when MiG planes of our air force - when I say "our," I mean the Yugoslav, the JNA air force - pushed back helicopters of the MUP of Croatia with national guards members who wanted to land in Obrovac and Knin?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that the essence of that intervention that the army should thereby prevent a great conflict from breaking out with the storming of these special troops, by their storming this area and coming into the territory in which the Serbs were living?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first and basic reason why the air force reacted was purely of a practical and formal nature. The -- these helicopter flights were not announced to the flight control system on a regular basis, according to regular procedure, and once they did come into contact with them, they gave the wrong coordinates. And this was the formal reason, regardless of the plane in question, was told to go back and land where it had taken off from. Now, this was investigated why they were sent back, but that was for legal reasons, according to the regulations. As far as my information told me, in the helicopter, Ustasha songs were being sung. They would sort of sing lyrics like, "We'll slaughter anybody who doesn't want to come with us," and that these special troops were being transported and flown in towards a police station, or I don't know what, to carry out the disarming. So that was the pretext for sending the helicopters back, although the legal provisions did exist for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can we know that we cannot claim at all that that particular operation on the part of the air force to stop the helicopters was any kind of form of incapacitation and to prevent the functioning of a Croatian state with the rule of law?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Croatian state violated the provisions and rules and regulations of the flight of helicopters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Milan Babic said here that they were stopped to prevent regular Croatian authorities from being able to function. That's what he said here.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he was in a position to give that kind of answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So there were other reasons. Second, tell me what you know about Pakrac. Or let me be more specific because we have to save time. Is it true that on the 2nd of March, 1999, in Pakrac, 600 members of the special units of the MUP of Croatia raided Serb houses, searched them, ransacked them, beat and mistreated the population and that the Serbs had to flee en masse?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of what you've just said is correct. That means that a forerunner to all this was the following: The Croats, members of that police station in Pakrac, following the principles of what had been done much earlier on in August in Knin, they were made to leave the station, and the resistance lay in the fact that they did not accept putting up the Croatian insignia, that is to say the chequerboard emblem, up on the police station building. So there was first of all this resistance on the part of the people in the police station, the policemen there, to accept these emblems that were being imposed by the current Croatian authorities. After that, what happened was that there was an intervention by 615 members of the special forces themselves, of the MUP of Croatia which were led by -- I don't know what his rank was then, he was probably an inspector, but his name was Markac. I think his first name was Stjepan. And when I arrived on the scene in Pakrac, what I came across was lots of policemen moving around in tens, groups of ten, like an army. There were lots of civilians put up against a wall that were being searched. I don't know that they stormed the houses, barged into the houses. I can't say that for sure. I don't recall that. And the fact that I was sent to Pakrac was because some Serbs which had fled from Pakrac had crossed over into Bosnian territory on the Bosnian side. And as far as I know from some secretary for national defence, they called up you or somebody else in Belgrade and said that they were in -- that 40 Serbs had been held in the Pakrac church and that they were going to slit their throats and set them on fire. And that's why the Federal Secretary for National Defence sent me to Pakrac in the first place, to check out and see what was going on there. The Serbs had not been locked up in the church, but the church was indeed a military facility, because up on the bell tower there was a sniper nest, a machine-gun nest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who had taken over this?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian MUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Croatian MUP took over the church and put a machine-gun nest up on the belfry; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Because it was at the high point from which you could control the whole of the town. And then the fact is that the Serbs from the nearby hill Kavarija started shooting at the police station and one MUP member was seriously wounded on that occasion. After that, there was in fact some shooting from the MUP APC. They were shooting at two soldiers who were providing security for ten combat vehicles that had come into Pakrac. There were some APCs and trucks, but there were no tanks yet, but they didn't meddle nor did they enter Pakrac. Then they shot at this little house, the hut where these two guards were on duty. And after that, the army entered Pakrac, those ten or 12 trucks and armoured vehicles which separated the Serb and Croatian forces. Otherwise, that night in Pakrac, Mr. Digoricija [phoen] was there, Mr. Digoricija, and he had taken over his duties as Deputy Minister of the Interior of Croatia. And we filed a criminal report against these two men, members of the combat vehicle for having opened fire, the APC, for having opened fire, which was -- but that was never realised because they were put away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who put them away?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP did, just like the ones from Trstenik who attacked me in 1999. And that -- those proceedings were never completed. So the MUP took care of them. After that, a meeting was held, attended by a portion of the Presidency, chaired by Mr. Mesic. Mr. Bucin was there too, and I think Bogic Bogicevic attended as well. Then there were some other responsible officials from the 5th Military District. I took part in the meeting, and the clash broke out because it was claimed that there were no refugees, no Serb refugees in the woods around Pakrac, who had taken to the woods. And I offered that I -- I said to Mr. Mesic that I would be willing to go and check it out for myself in the field, and that's where I came into conflict with him personally. Well, the situation calmed down after that. The forces were separated, and that's the story as I know it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, can we draw a very short and clear conclusion: The army exclusively carried out the separation of forces, the conflicting forces.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely so. And had it not done so, there would have been a major conflict because they were sandwiched between the MUP forces and the Serb forces. But once the army entered Pakrac, the shooting stopped and 40 members of the MUP were arrested, as well as some other Serbs who they probably thought had -- were from the SDS, and they were transferred to Bjelovar. And the condition for the station to go back to normal was that the Croatian MUP should return -- have those 40 Serbs returned to Pakrac. And they were indeed returned, but as far as I could see, they had been beaten up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They had all been beaten up?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say they had all been beaten up, but I did see some injured people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that after that particular operation, the kind performed by the Croatian MUP in Pakrac, that they carried out a similar operation at the Plitvice lakes, Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I said that that was my impression when I talked to people, that after that Pakrac, they took courage and -- to launch broader military action. And the MUP of Croatia, ever since Pakrac, started to behave as a Croatian army. They marched in three columns out of Zagreb in a complete military formation. In Pakrac, they deployed the army according to the principles of army deployment and not as MUPs; they would march in platoons, et cetera. And in my opinion, that was the first step towards legalising the future Croatian armed forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you mean legalisation?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they came out with 615 members of the police force, which acted in fact as an army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was a demonstration, in fact, of working as an army. It wasn't legalisation. There was nothing legal in it.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can use whichever term you liked, but the legalisation actually took place in June when the ZNG came out onto the stadium and there was a review of troops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to Plitvice and the JNA role there, is it true and correct that from the 10th Corps in Zagreb at Plitvice after the conflicts between the ZNG, the National Guards Corps, and the local inhabitants of Serb ethnicity, that only a small group was sent of experienced security organs in order to attend the situation in the field and to collect information, to reconnoiter and gather information?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't quite like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was it, then?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: The principle is when a military unit goes out into the field, then the security organs move with it. Now, they were there first of all because a large portion of the units had gone out into the area to separate the Serb and Croatian --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's precisely what I'm asking you about. Is it true that when the conflict at Plitvice took place between the ZNG and the local inhabitants, the JNA only went there to separate the two sides and to calm the situation, that it didn't side with anybody?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely so. Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on, then.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that first commander, the commander was a general, and he was a Croat. He was an ethnic Croat. Otherwise, there were several generals. They replaced each other. And one of them was General Raseta.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that on the 2nd of May a similar operation, they intended to launch a similar operation in Borovo Selo, that is to say the MUP members, with their attack on Borovo Selo, that they were intending to do the same thing?
