utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't in the security department in Belgrade in May. I don't really know. I don't have any specific information as something that I took part in, but I do, of course, know that a unit did intervene. I think it was a unit from Osijek, in actual fact. Once again, they went to separate the two warring sides, that is to say the ZNG on the one side and the armed Serbs on the other in that particular area, and that people opened fire on the column once it had left Osijek, the military column, as it emerged from Osijek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember, or perhaps you can confirm the fact that after that, on the 29th of June, radio Vukovar appealed to all Croat males to respond to checkpoints and collection points with their long weapons, long-barrelled weapons.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was broadcast over the radio. Everybody knew about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know about Zvonko Kostic from Vukovar and a statement he made that a list had already been compiled for the liquidation of prominent Serbs from the area of Eastern Slavonia? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that event took place quite a lot earlier, seven or eight months prior to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm saying, before.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but considerably before. So we uncovered this piece of information in December 1990 and had all the material to support it, to support our claims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This -- these lists for silent liquidations, for expulsions, for dismissals and so on and so forth, they date back to 1990 until the clash broke out, the conflict broke out; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know about these two cases, specific cases which we've already mentioned, Zvonko Ostojic and the other man Damir from the Hrvatska Uzdanica about the lists for liquidation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that in August 1991, two soldiers were killed and one officer wounded on the 25th, six soldiers and officers in Vukovar were wounded as well? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that, before that, the barracks in Vukovar were blocked by the Croatian National Guard Corps and cut off so that the officers and soldiers did not have any electricity, water, any supplies for 20 days? And not only was it blocked, it was also attacked with different projectiles, and that already on the 14th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: General -- I'm going to interrupt you. I thought you said, General, earlier that you did not know about Vukovar because you had left the service, but I may be wrong about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you couldn't be wrong, but I was an active-duty serviceman when this was taking place in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, we're talking about 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me repeat my question to you. Is it true that before that, the barracks in Vukovar had been blocked by the Croatian National Guards Corps and that they were kept without electricity, water, or other supplies for a period of 20 days, during which time they were attacked by different projectiles and that already on the 14th of September, among the JNA members, there were persons who were dead and wounded? They had no water, no food, and quite simply they were under a complete blockade. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are a lot of questions in what you've just asked me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, tell us what is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let the witness deal with these things one at a time. It's not fair on anybody the way that you pile them up like this. The first question, General, was this: Is it right that the barracks in Vukovar were blocked by the ZNG for a period of 20 days?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I say that before the events that I talked about, that it had been already under a blockade for 20 days.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I please answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two soldiers -- the two soldiers who were killed that the accused just mentioned were killed as they were going into town. And at the time, the barracks were still not under a complete blockade. On the 14th of September, however, 1991, a telegram arrived which was brought into the meeting that was taking place of the staff with General Kadijevic, and I attended that staff meeting. It was a very dramatic telegram, to say that the Vukovar barracks had been under blockade for already 20 days and that they had spent up all their reserves of food, water supplies, and so on, that there were a number of wounded persons whom they were not able to give assistance to, and that there were a number of people who had been killed as well, that they were unable to bury their dead because they were unable to go out into the compound and had to keep them wrapped up in sheets, and that the stench from the decaying bodies had a very negative effect on the psychology of those present, on the members. And the General Staff was prevailed upon to lend assistance to them. General Kadijevic ordered Admiral Brovet to leave the meeting straight away and to call up, I think it was Wijnaendts, and to convey to Franjo Tudjman that unless he take action immediately - and these were his words - unless he deblocks the Vukovar barracks straight away, immediately, there would be a large scale war on his hands. Admiral Brovet returned to the meeting and said that he had conveyed the message to Mr. Wijnaendts. I can't be absolutely sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me remind you. And that he had asked for patience, for the General Staff to show patience over the next 24 hours. After that, he informed General Raseta from Zagreb that General Aksentijevic, with seven Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. others, seven other officers, had been arrested, and they were coming back from an assignment they had been on, an official assignment, and that he had been told by some top people in the Croatian leadership that Tudjman had said that Croatia was defending itself at Vukovar and that it was not attacking anybody. And on the next day, the 15th of September, larger units of the JNA were on the move and the order was given to deblock the barracks. So that is what I can testify to, my part in it, because I was a participant, and that's what I remember very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is not at all being disputed that on the 14th of September when this telegram arrived, the barracks had already been under a blockade for 20 days with members inside who were being killed and wounded, with no electricity, no water, in a situation that was so bad that they were not even able to bury their dead because they couldn't leave the -- go out into the compound because there was shooting coming from all sides; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said. And the next day, on that 15th of September, a general blockade of all military facilities in Croatia was under way. So as of the 15th of September, all the military facilities were under a blockade, as well as the command of the air force in -- and headquarters in Zagreb. The whole Varazdin Corps was blocked and it surrendered on the 21st of September, as far as I recall. And the garrison in Bjelovar stayed on for another seven days. It offered resistance during that time. That was the garrison in which Major Stjepic blew up the warehouse because he didn't want to surrender. And that is the same garrison where, after the HDZ stormed the barracks, in front of a column of soldiers, their commander was shot, the political advisor and the security organ. They were all shot in front of the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, can we then note that a blockade of all the barracks in Croatia was carried out then on the basis of a decision made by the Croatian leadership? Can we say that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that Brovet, after talks -- the talks you talked about with Lord Carrington, which he was charged to do by Kadijevic, said that Carrington would like to convey a message to Kadijevic and say that the JNA should refrain from any operations over the next 24 hours so that he could reach an agreement with Tudjman to deblock the barracks. Is it true that the JNA respected that time period, it waited for this 24-hour deadline for these others, that is to say Lord Carrington and Tudjman, to reach an agreement on the deblocking of the barracks and that it intervened only after a clear-cut stand, and when they saw quite clearly that the barracks would not be deblocked and the barracks was in the situation that you've described? Is it true that it adhered to that 24-hour deadline?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I said that the preparations to deblock the barracks began on the 15th of September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did this JNA operation have any other goal and objective except to deblock the barracks?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the first objective, and that's the one I know about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you happen to have any knowledge as to how the soldiers in Vukovar were killed and how the bodies of the dead soldiers in Vukovar were inundated with fuel and set fire to by the paramilitaries, the event that took place there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know about that partially. I know about the members of the military police who were killed in that first onslaught when they entered Vukovar. And I know from earlier on as well, from the period when we worked to uncover the illegal channels in which weapons were being brought into Croatia. May I just complete my answer, please. So before that, there was a campaign, and a party meeting when Vuk Draskovic said that the Serb lands were everywhere where Serb graves exist. I don't know if you remember that or not. Anyway, then the leadership of the HDZ in Osijek, with Seks at its head, made a decision that the JNA members who had been killed on Croatian territory should not be buried, because then Serbs would come to visit their graves, because that's what Vuk Draskovic had previously said. And then the decision was taken that they should be burnt, that their bodies should be burnt. Now, the elements of what I'm saying now are to be found partially in a diary of Marin Vidic, kept by Marin Vidic. And he was the commander of the Crisis Staff for the defence of Vukovar. He was taken prisoner and that diary was confiscated and handed over to the law courts. So there were instances where the dead bodies of soldiers were in fact burnt. How many I can't really say with any precision. I know that on that first onslaught about 20 JNA members were killed and wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must draw the hearing to a close. It's past time and there is another case coming in this afternoon. Mr. Milosevic, you have now, so that you could complete your preparation over the weekend, you have four and a quarter hours left for this witness, and you must tailor your cross-examination to allow you to finish in that time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. I asked you yesterday, however, whether you were going to give me some more time on Tuesday. What you're saying now means that you're just giving me Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That's the position.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But then that is a total of less than two and a half days, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's a total -- it's a total of practically eight hours, which is slightly more than the Prosecution will have had. Yes. We will adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 17th day of February, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
